summaries.example: Imagine seeing your friend across the playground. You might be sure it is your friend, but then discover it was someone else wearing a similar coat. Cook Wilson called this being “under the impression” that something is true. He separated this from knowing, because real knowledge must fit the facts.
summaries.summary: John Cook Wilson was an Oxford philosopher whose work helped begin Oxford Realism. He studied ancient philosophy, logic, perception, knowledge, language, and morality. His most important idea was that knowing is not simply believing something with extra confidence or evidence. Knowledge is its own kind of mental state, and it must be connected with the facts. He also argued that we usually perceive real objects directly, rather than first seeing private copies in our minds. To study philosophy, he recommended looking closely at ordinary language and concrete cases instead of starting with very abstract theories. His ideas strongly influenced Oxford teachers and later philosophers, even though his name became less well known.
key_ideas: Cook Wilson said knowledge is different from belief. Feeling very sure does not automatically make a belief knowledge.
He thought careful attention to ordinary words and everyday examples could help philosophers avoid confusing theories.
He defended the idea that perception puts us in contact with real objects, not only with inner mental copies.
He described qualities as belonging to particular things while also being shared across examples.
His teaching influenced Oxford philosophy, including ordinary language philosophy and moral intuitionism.
summaries.why_it_matters: Cook Wilson helps us notice that being confident, guessing, believing, and knowing may not be the same thing. His ideas also encourage us to test big theories against ordinary examples. Questions about real objects, knowledge, and the meaning of words still matter whenever people decide what to trust or how to explain their experiences.

important_terms.definition: A direct noticing or understanding of something, without needing a long chain of reasons.
Being sure that something is true because it is actually true, not just because it feels convincing.
A strong feeling that something is true, even though it may not be knowledge.
The view that we can perceive real things themselves, rather than only pictures or copies inside our minds.
A feature that can belong to many particular things, such as redness or triangular shape.

questions_to_think_about: Can you feel certain about something and still be mistaken?
Is seeing a red apple seeing the apple itself or an image in your mind?
Why might everyday words help us think about difficult questions?

summaries.example: Suppose you see someone from behind and immediately take the person to be your friend. You act on that impression without considering alternatives, then learn that it was a stranger. Cook Wilson distinguished this state from judgement and knowledge: you did not carefully decide on evidence, and your certainty did not guarantee truth. The case shows why a mental feeling of confidence cannot by itself define knowledge.
summaries.summary: John Cook Wilson was an Oxford classicist, mathematician, and philosopher whose teaching helped generate Oxford Realism. His central work concerned the theory of knowledge. He held that knowledge is factive—knowing that p requires p to be true—and that it is not definable as belief with added justification, certainty, or evidence. Knowledge and belief therefore do not share a basic mental state that becomes one or the other through external conditions. He connected knowledge with apprehension, a direct grasp that can serve as a non-inferential foundation, while distinguishing it from judgement, opinion, and the unreflective condition of being under an impression. In perception, he rejected mental intermediaries and defended a form of direct realism: what is apprehended is the object itself, not a copy produced in consciousness. His method emphasized ordinary language and detailed examples, though he allowed that ordinary usage might need correction. In metaphysics, he discussed universals through particularized qualities, anticipating aspects of later trope theories. He also criticized modern symbolic logic, often unsuccessfully, while offering a more interesting diagnosis of Lewis Carroll’s regress about rules of inference. His influence continued through Prichard, Ryle, Austin, and later philosophers such as McDowell, Travis, and Williamson.
key_ideas: Knowledge is factive and not analyzable as justified true belief or belief plus a further common ingredient.
Cook Wilson rejected a shared “highest common factor” that could appear as knowledge in one case and belief in another.
His direct realism denies that perception requires an epistemic intermediary such as a mental image or sense-datum.
He distinguished apprehension, judgement, opinion, belief, and the unreflective state of being under an impression.
His account of universals combines particularized qualities with a realist claim that universals are genuinely present in particulars.
His teaching helped move Oxford away from idealism and influenced ordinary language philosophy and Oxford moral intuitionism.
summaries.why_it_matters: Cook Wilson’s work raises lasting questions about whether knowledge is more basic than belief, whether perception reaches the world without representational intermediaries, and how language reflects distinctions in thought. His successes and mistakes are both instructive: his careful analyses influenced major philosophical traditions, while his rejection of modern logic showed how a powerful method can coexist with serious technical errors.

important_terms.definition: A non-derivative grasp of a fact; Cook Wilson treated apprehension as a foundation for knowledge, though he did not give it a full definition.
A factive, sui generis mental state: if someone knows that p, then p is true, and knowing is not reducible to belief plus another ingredient.
A state distinct from knowledge, often involving confidence but not necessarily truth; it is not simply a weaker form of knowledge.
The position that perception concerns objects themselves rather than mental representations that serve as intermediaries.
A view of particulars as particularized qualities, while also holding that a universal is something identical in its instances rather than mere resemblance.
The use of ordinary words and concrete cases as evidence for distinctions in thought, while allowing ordinary language to be corrected or improved.
The idea that a sentence’s contribution to truth depends partly on the question, emphasis, or situation in which it is used.

questions_to_think_about: If knowledge cannot be defined using belief and justification, what explains the difference between knowing and merely believing?
Does direct realism explain illusion and hallucination, or does it need additional distinctions?
Can ordinary language reveal philosophical truths without making ordinary usage infallible?
What is the difference between a logical subject and a thing that possesses an attribute?
Does the case of being under an impression successfully explain error?

summaries.example: You notice a backpack in the hallway and immediately think it belongs to Maya. You do not compare clues or consider other possibilities; you simply act as if it is hers. Later, Maya says it belongs to someone else. Cook Wilson would call your first state being under the impression that it was Maya’s. It was not exactly a judgement, because you had not weighed evidence, and it was not knowledge, because it was false.
summaries.summary: John Cook Wilson was an Oxford philosopher whose teaching became a major source of Oxford Realism. His main concern was how people know things. He argued that knowledge is factive: a person cannot know that a claim is true unless it is true. He also rejected the common idea that knowledge is simply belief plus justification or extra certainty. For him, knowing, believing, opining, and judging were different activities of thought. He described apprehension as a direct grasp that can ground reasoning, and he examined cases in which people act confidently while merely being under an impression. Cook Wilson also defended direct realism about perception. He denied that we first perceive inner copies and then infer the existence of outside objects. Instead, he held that the object itself is what is apprehended. His philosophical method began with ordinary words and concrete examples, although he believed ordinary language could sometimes be improved. In his discussion of universals, he proposed that qualities are particularized in individual things while retaining a real identity across those things. He made serious mistakes in rejecting much modern mathematical logic, but he offered a notable explanation of why putting a rule of inference into an argument can create an endless regress. His influence reached later Oxford philosophers and continues in debates about knowledge, perception, and language.
key_ideas: Cook Wilson argued that knowledge and belief are different kinds of mental state, not points on one scale of confidence.
He thought knowledge is factive: if you know that something is the case, it really is the case.
He used ordinary language and particular examples to challenge overly abstract philosophical theories.
His direct realism rejected the idea that we perceive objects only through mental pictures or sense-data.
He treated universals as real in particulars, while describing particulars through particularized qualities.
His students and followers helped shape Oxford Realism, ordinary language philosophy, and moral intuitionism.
summaries.why_it_matters: The entry shows how one philosopher’s careful attention to everyday cases can challenge broad theories about the mind and world. Cook Wilson’s distinctions help us ask whether confidence is enough for knowledge, whether perception connects us directly with reality, and whether the meaning of a sentence depends on its use. These questions remain important in school, science, public discussion, and everyday decisions.

important_terms.definition: A direct grasp of something that can provide a starting point for reasoning, rather than a conclusion reached from other reasons.
A mental state that must be true when someone really knows a fact; Cook Wilson said it cannot be reduced to belief.
Taking something to be true, often with confidence, without having the kind of certainty that knowledge requires.
A decision reached after doubt or consideration of evidence; Cook Wilson separated it from simple apprehension.
The view that perception gives us the real object, rather than only an inner representation caused by it.
A feature shared by different examples, such as triangularity in several triangular objects.
Studying how people ordinarily use words and examples in order to uncover distinctions that theories can overlook.

questions_to_think_about: Is a very well-supported belief always knowledge?
What might be lost if philosophers ignore the way people normally use words?
Can we explain an illusion while still saying that ordinary perception reaches real objects?
Are qualities like redness real features of things, or only names we give to similar experiences?
Why might a rule of reasoning fail to explain, by itself, why someone actually makes an inference?
